item.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.27147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(\beta, \delta)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^\beta, \beta \in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-\delta}),\delta \in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $\beta > 1, \delta>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $\beta\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $\beta > \delta + k(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $\beta > \delta + (k-1)(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.
item.dc:creator: Kiril Bangachev

item.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2610.27168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm. We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $\tau$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,\tau,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.
item.dc:creator: Markus Bl\"aser, Pranjal Dutta, Sagnik Dutta, Gorav Jindal

item.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $\alpha_{GW}+\tilde{\Omega}(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $\alpha_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm \epsilon$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.
item.dc:creator: Rares-Darius Buhai, Suprovat Ghoshal, Pravesh Kothari, Euiwoong Lee, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev

item.title: Parameterizing Cluster Editing by the Number of Deletions
item.description: arXiv:2610.27289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Cluster Editing, we are given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$ and ask whether at most $k$ edge insertions and deletions turn $G$ into a disjoint union of cliques. Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked in 2012 at MFCS whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number $\ell$ of edge deletions, a parameter based on the solution rather than on the structure of the input graph. We answer this question negatively: Cluster Editing with at most $k$ edits, at most $\ell$ of which are deletions, is W[1]-hard with respect to $\ell$, even when combined with the pathwidth and the feedback edge set number of the input graph. The hardness extends to editing towards $H$-free graphs for every graph $H$ that is a clique minus one edge on at least four vertices. On the positive side, we show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when $\ell$ is combined with the excess $\mu$ of $k$ over the lower bound given by a packing of modification-disjoint induced paths on three vertices, a lower bound that state-of-the-art solvers use. Each of the two parameters alone leads to intractability, but together they admit an $O(4^{\mu+\ell}\cdot(n+m+\mu))$-time algorithm and a problem kernel with $O((\ell+\mu)^2)$ vertices. Both results extend to packings of stars and the algorithm extends to $H$-free editing.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Froese, Leon Kellerhals, Frank Sommer, Manuel Sorge, Ond\v{r}ej Such\'y

item.title: Approximating Directed Telephone Multicast
item.description: arXiv:2610.27422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the telephone model a message starts at a source vertex, and in every round each informed vertex may call one neighbour. Telephone multicast asks for a schedule that informs a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. On directed graphs, the best known ratio for this problem was $\tilde O(\sqrt k)$, due to Elkin and Kortsarz and to Hathcock, Kortsarz and Ravi. For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm with running time $n^{O(\ell)}$ that computes a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)\cdot(\mathrm{OPT}+k^{1/\ell})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $\mathrm{OPT}$ the optimum. Since $\mathrm{OPT}\ge\log_2(k+1)$, this gives ratio $O(k^{\epsilon})$ in time $n^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, and ratio $O(\log^4k)$ in quasi-polynomial time. The method rests on jump trees with additive vertex loads, a height reduction that bounds the load of every vertex, and a recursive greedy algorithm with an exponential potential. We also show that directed multicast is a special case of the degree-bounded directed Steiner tree problem on a time-expanded digraph. With known algorithms for that problem this gives randomized ratios $O(\log^2n)$ in time $n^{O(\log n)}$ and $O(n^\epsilon)$ in time $n^{O(1/\epsilon)}$, which, unlike ours, grow with $n$. On the hardness side, directed multicast stays $(1-\epsilon)\ln k$-hard even when $\mathrm{OPT}=O(\log k)$, the regime in which the previous algorithms were weakest.
item.dc:creator: Shahin Kamali, Seyed-Mohammad Seyed-Javadi

item.title: A 2/3-Approximation Algorithm for the Residual Maximum Matching Problem in General Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The residual maximum matching problem asks for a maximum matching whose deletion leaves a graph with the largest possible matching number. For unweighted graphs, previous work provides a $1/2$-approximation guarantee in general graphs and a $2/3$ guarantee in graphs with a perfect matching. We present a $2/3$-approximation algorithm running in $O(n^5)$ time, extending the latter guarantee to general graphs. The algorithm improves the residual matching number through single-edge exchanges involving free vertices. We prove that, for any maximum matching that admits no further improvement by such exchanges, the residual matching number is at least $2/3$ of the optimum, and we give an example showing that this bound is tight.
item.dc:creator: Quanlong Niu, Riheng Jia

item.title: An Exact Polynomial-Time Algorithm for the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.27838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem seeks to disconnect two designated terminals with minimum total power by assigning powers to graph vertices and deleting every edge for which the sum of the powers at its endpoints reaches its edge weight. Previous work gave a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, while its exact computational complexity remained open. We prove that general MSPEC with nonnegative edge weights can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Specifically, we first use linear programming duality for each fixed cut to reformulate MSPEC as minimizing the maximum terminal-relaxed matching weight over all $s$-$t$ cuts. Then, we construct a terminal-copy extended graph that transforms the maximum-weight matching model with unconstrained terminal capacities for a fixed cut into an equivalent ordinary maximum-weight matching model. Next, we extend the submodularity of the unweighted maximum-matching cut function to nonnegative edge weights and prove that the restriction obtained by fixing the terminal copies on prescribed sides remains submodular. Consequently, MSPEC reduces to exact submodular function minimization. Once an optimal cut is obtained, a corresponding optimal power assignment can be recovered. This result resolves the open question concerning the exact computational complexity of general MSPEC.
item.dc:creator: Quanlong Niu, Wei Liang, Riheng Jia, Zhao Zhang

item.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Results for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.27935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem (MEG-Set), which asks for a minimum-cardinality set $M$ of vertices of an undirected graph $G$ of $n$ vertices such that every edge of $G$ belongs to all shortest paths between some pair of vertices in $M$. We present new approximation and hardness results for MEG-Set. On the positive side, we design a deterministic polynomial-time $O(n^{1/3}\log^{2/3}n)$-approximation algorithm, improving upon the previously best-known $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ approximation ratio. On the negative side, for every constant $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we prove that the problem admits no polynomial-time $\big(2^{\log^{1-\varepsilon} n}\big)$-approximation algorithm, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq \mathsf{DTIME}(n^{\operatorname{polylog} n})$. This substantially improves upon the previously known logarithmic inapproximability bound. We also prove that \megset is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard on planar $2$-degenerate graphs, whereas $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness was previously known for $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs. We conclude by observing a connection between monitoring edge-geodetic sets and subsetwise distance preservers, i.e., subgraphs that preserve distances between all pairs of vertices in $S\subseteq V(G)$. Specifically, we show that any upper bound on the size of the latter yields a lower bound on the size of the former.
item.dc:creator: Davide Bil\`o, Giordano Colli, Stefano Leucci

item.title: ARRIVAL in cube-root subexponential time
item.description: arXiv:2610.28241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the ARRIVAL problem, a token travels through a switch digraph: at every vertex, it leaves along one of two out-arcs, and the two are used alternately. The question is which of two terminals the token reaches first. ARRIVAL lies in $\mathsf{NP} \cap \mathsf{coNP}$, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known.The fastest known algorithms turn some vertices into terminals and search for consistent guesses of the numbers of tokens that these vertices send out. The first, due to G\"artner et al. [ICALP 2021], searches all vertices at once with an algorithm for fixed points of monotone maps, and the second, due to Haslebacher [ICALP 2025], searches one vertex at a time by binary search. Both search for a fixed point of the same map, which returns how many tokens arrive at the guessed vertices. We guess the vertices in blocks of $k$, between these two extremes, which needs a search in $k$ dimensions with few evaluations of this map. To do so, we build on the connection between ARRIVAL and $\ell_1$-contractions established in the second of these works. We search with $\ell_1$-centerpoints of the remaining guesses, which are guaranteed to exist by Haslebacher et al. [FOCS 2025], and which we approximate deterministically. In order to prove our results, we show how to find the least fixed points of maps from $\{0, \ldots, N\}^k$ to itself that have unit increments. For ARRIVAL on $n$-vertex switch digraphs, this gives run time $2^{\mathcal{O}(n^{1/3} \cdot \log^{2/3} n)}$, improving the previous time bound of $n^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})}$. We work with the more general \garrival problem, with many tokens and several terminals, and solve it in the same time when there are at most $2^n$ tokens.
item.dc:creator: Ebrahim Ghorbani, Raul Lopes, Matthias Mnich

item.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.28501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. This models deliveries from a common depot in which each customer's order must be delivered in a single trip. UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved through several recent advances; in particular, Zhao and Xiao (2026) recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. In this paper, we give a deterministic $(5/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in $n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}$ time for every rational $0<\varepsilon\le1/9$, applicable to general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We combine these routes with those obtained by matching and set packing, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity.
item.dc:creator: Zhenyu Wang

item.title: Diverse Schedules for Makespan Minimization on Unrelated Machines
item.description: arXiv:2610.28514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study makespan minimization on unrelated machines with the additional goal of constructing diverse schedules: Instead of outputting a single schedule, we seek a collection of schedules with provable makespan guarantees and substantially different job assignments. Committing to a single schedule in advance may be undesirable. Processing times may be uncertain, and constraints or domain knowledge may emerge later, so $k$ schedules of similar quality offer meaningful alternatives. We measure pairwise diversity by the weighted Hamming distance between job assignments and study the two standard objectives in the diverse-solutions literature: max-sum diversity, which maximizes the total pairwise distance between schedules, and max-min diversity, which maximizes the smallest pairwise distance. For the max-sum objective, we show that optimal diversity can be achieved in polynomial time without sacrificing the classic makespan approximation factor. For every feasible makespan target $T$, we can compute $k$ schedules of makespan at most $2T$ whose max-sum diversity is optimal among all $k$ schedules of makespan at most $T$. Therefore, we match the classic factor-$2$ makespan guarantee of Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (Math. Prog., 1990) and preserve optimal diversity. For the max-min objective, we show that the diversity problem is inherently harder. Namely, we show that, even without makespan constraints, deciding whether three schedules of given pairwise diversity exist is NP-hard. We complete this with two complementary bicriteria approximation algorithms for every fixed $k$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$. The first preserves almost all of the optimal max-min diversity with makespan at most $(3\lceil12/\varepsilon\rceil+1)T$. The second keeps the makespan arbitrarily close to the classic $2$ guarantee while achieving a $\frac{1}{2}(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the optimal max-min diversity.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Bruchhold, Matthias Mnich, Karolina Tammemaa, Morten Weber, Michalis Xefteris, Bart Zondervan

item.title: Dynamic Distances Without Matrix Inverse
item.description: arXiv:2610.28573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fully dynamic exact distance problem in unweighted directed graphs, where the graph undergoes edge insertions and deletions, and the distance between two query vertices must be reported. Under the combinatorial Boolean matrix multiplication conjecture, any subquadratic-time algorithm for this problem must use algebraic techniques. All prior work uses the polynomial matrix inverse as its algebraic tool, but within subquadratic time, this technique can only maintain distances up to a small-polynomial hop bound. So larger distances must be reassembled from short-range pieces by a combinatorial layer. This hybrid algebraic-combinatorial construction has led to a substantial slowdown for dynamic distances compared to other dynamic graph problems relying on algebraic techniques. We give the first subquadratic-time dynamic distance algorithm built on dynamically maintaining a different algebraic object than the matrix inverse. By maintaining the Frobenius form $A=KCK^{-1}$ of a dynamic generic (i.e., cyclic) matrix $A$, we can query all the powers $A^\ell = K C^\ell K^{-1}$ efficiently. For adjacency matrix~$A$, the smallest $\ell$ with $(A^\ell)_{s,t}\neq 0$ is the $st$-distance in the associated graph. So, unlike dynamic matrix inverse, we get distance information directly without hop truncation, and we no longer need to perform any combinatorial reassembly. This purely algebraic approach to dynamic distances leads to the fastest dynamic distance algorithm with $O(n^{1.58})$ update time. The earlier use of the Frobenius form maintained the dense change of basis $K$ explicitly and required $\tilde O (n^2)$ time per update [KS23]. Our key observation is that this change of basis is highly structured, which lets us maintain it implicitly. This gives the first subquadratic dynamic algorithm for the Frobenius normal form and characteristic polynomial for generic matrices.
item.dc:creator: Jan van den Brand, Adam Karczmarz, Aryan Patel

item.title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
item.description: arXiv:2610.27402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.
item.dc:creator: Lunjia Hu, Anish Jayant, Peter Li, Princewill Okoroafor, Abhishek Shetty

item.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.27451v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.
item.dc:creator: Greg Sidebottom

item.title: Improved rapid phase ordering for Ising dynamics on random regular graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27673v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs with $n$ vertices at low temperature, in the regime $\beta \geq C/d$ where $C,d$ are sufficiently large constants. In this regime, the full mixing time is exponential in $n$, because of the bottleneck between the two dominant phases: configurations with a majority of plus spins and configurations with a majority of minus spins. We show that, for sufficiently large $d$, if the dynamics is initialized with an excess of at least $\epsilon_{C,d} n$ plus spins over minus spins, then it quasi-equilibrates in time $O(\log n)$ to the Gibbs measure conditioned on positive magnetization. In addition, the required bias $\epsilon_{C,d}$ can be chosen so that $\epsilon_{C,d}\to 0$ as $d,C\to\infty$. Previous bound of \cite{GSS25+} in the Ising and large-$d$ setting required $\beta \gtrsim (\log d)/d$. A key difficulty is that, even from the all-plus initialization, one must control the propagation of negative information in spacetime in a low-temperature model with strong local correlations. We address this by developing a new bootstrap approach to proving subcriticality of disagreement clusters under the grand coupling.
item.dc:creator: Zhangsong Li, Allan Sly

item.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
item.description: arXiv:2610.27956v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $\Theta(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.
item.dc:creator: Rishi Advani, Abolfazl Asudeh

item.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2610.28141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang

item.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.28213v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.
item.dc:creator: Argyrios Deligkas, Eduard Eiben, Robert Ganian, Tiger-Lily Goldsmith, Marlene Gr\"undel, Simon Wietheger

item.title: Birthday Estimators Are Uniformly Optimal for Renyi Entropy
item.description: arXiv:2610.28581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collisions are a basic probe of unknown distributions, used for testing and for counting substructures in graphs, and they underlie R\'enyi entropy, a fundamental measure of uncertainty with applications in cryptography, machine learning, physics, and biology. Motivated by this, we study the natural birthday estimator. We prove Bernstein-type concentration for it and show that it is minimax optimal, uniformly and jointly in alphabet size, order, accuracy, and confidence, with no sample splitting, clipping, or median aggregation. This, in particular, settles the sample complexity of integer-order R\'enyi entropy estimation up to absolute constants in all regimes, closing the gap between the best known upper and lower bounds. Our concentration bound rests on a sensitivity analysis of collision count, and the matching lower bound on a sharp analysis of detecting a hidden spike in a plateau distribution.
item.dc:creator: Maciej Sk\'orski

item.title: Shaving Logs via Large Sieve Inequality: Faster Algorithms for Sparse Convolution and More
item.description: arXiv:2403.20326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In sparse convolution-type problems, a common technique is to hash the input integers modulo a random prime $p\in [Q/2,Q]$ for some parameter $Q$, which reduces the range of the input integers while preserving their additive structure. However, this hash family suffers from two drawbacks, which led to bottlenecks in many state-of-the-art algorithms: (1) The collision probability of two elements from $[N]$ is $O(\frac{\log N}{Q})$ rather than $O(\frac{1}{Q})$; (2) It is difficult to derandomize the choice of $p$; known derandomization techniques lead to super-logarithmic overhead [Chan, Lewenstein STOC'15]. In this paper, we partially overcome these drawbacks in certain scenarios, via novel applications of the large sieve inequality from analytic number theory. Consequently, we obtain the following improved algorithms for various problems (in the standard word RAM model): Sparse Nonnegative Convolution: We obtain an $O(t\log t)$-time Las Vegas algorithm that computes the convolution $A\star B$ of two nonnegative integer vectors $A,B$, where $t$ is the output sparsity $\|A\star B\|_0$. Moreover, our algorithm terminates in $O(t\log t)$ time with $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(t)$ probability. Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances: Given a length-$m$ pattern $P$ and a length-$n$ text $T$, we obtain a deterministic $O(n\sqrt{m\log \log m})$-time algorithm that exactly computes the Hamming distance between $P$ and every length-$m$ substring of $T$. Sparse General Convolution: We also give a Monte Carlo $O(t\log t)$ time algorithm for sparse convolution with possibly negative input in the restricted case where the length $N$ of the input vectors satisfies $N\le t^{1.99}$.
item.dc:creator: Ce Jin, Yinzhan Xu

item.title: ${\varepsilon}$-Cost Sharding: Scaling Hypergraph-Based Data Structures to Trillions of Keys
item.description: arXiv:2503.18397v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe a simple and yet very scalable implementation of static functions (VFunc) and of static filters (VFilter) based on hypergraphs. We introduce the idea of $\varepsilon$-cost sharding, which allows us to build structures that can manage trillions of keys, at the same time increasing memory locality in hypergraph-based constructions. Contrarily to the commonly used HEM sharding method, $\varepsilon$-cost sharding does not require to store of additional information, and does not introduce dependencies in the computation chain; its only cost is that of few arithmetical instructions, and of a relative increase $\varepsilon$ in space usage. We apply $\varepsilon$-cost sharding to the classical MWHC construction, but we obtain the best result by combining Dietzfelbinger and Walzer's fuse graphs for large shards with lazy Gaussian elimination for small shards. We obtain large structures with an overhead of 10.5% with respect to the information-theoretical lower bound and with a query time that is a few nanoseconds away from the query time of the non-sharded version, which is the fastest currently available within the same space bounds. Besides comparing our structures with a non-sharded version, we contrast its tradeoffs with bumped ribbon constructions, a space-saving alternative to hypergraph-based static functions and filters, which provide optimum space consumption but slow construction and query time (though construction can be parallelized very efficiently). We build offline a trillion-key filter using commodity hardware in just 60 ns/key. Finally, we show that $\varepsilon$-cost sharding and fuse graphs carry over with no effort to data structures that reduce to static functions, such as monotone minimal perfect hash functions and compressed static functions.
item.dc:creator: Sebastiano Vigna

item.title: Algorithms for Computing Longest Unbordered Factors on Run-Length Encoded Strings
item.description: arXiv:2507.16285v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A border of a string is a non-empty proper prefix of the string that is also a suffix. A string is called unbordered if it has no border. The longest unbordered factor is a fundamental notion in stringology, closely related to string periodicity. This paper addresses the longest unbordered factor problem: given a string of length $n$, the goal is to compute its longest factor that is unbordered. While recent work has achieved subquadratic and near-linear time algorithms for this problem, the best known worst-case time complexity remains $O(n \log n)$ [Kociumaka et al., ISAAC 2018]. In this paper, we investigate the problem in the context of compressed string processing, focusing specifically on run-length encoded (RLE) strings. We first present a simple yet crucial structural observation relating unbordered factors and RLE-compressed strings. Building on this, we propose an algorithm that solves the problem in $O(m^{1.5} \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m \log^2 m)$ space, where $m$ is the size of the RLE-compressed input string. Furthermore, we propose another algorithm for the problem that runs in average $O(m \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m\log m)$ space: The average-case bound holds under an exponent-bounded random-input model, in which the input is chosen uniformly from the strings of RLE size $m$ whose run exponents are at most a given bound $E\geq 2$. Our approaches extend key ideas from [Gawrychowski et al., SPIRE 2015] to the RLE setting through new combinatorial insights. When the RLE size $m$ is sufficiently small compared to $n$, our algorithms achieve linear-time behavior in $n$, potentially leading to improved performance over existing methods in such cases.
item.dc:creator: Shoma Sekizaki, Takuya Mieno

item.title: Improved Online Load Balancing in the Two-Norm
item.description: arXiv:2511.03345v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the online load balancing problem on unrelated machines, with the objective of minimizing the square of the $\ell_2$ norm of the loads on the machines. The greedy algorithm of Awerbuch et al. (STOC'95) is optimal for deterministic algorithms and achieves a competitive ratio of $3 + 2 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.828$, and an improved $5$-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding has been shown by Caragiannis (SODA'08). In this work, we present the first algorithm breaking the barrier of $5$ on the competitive ratio, achieving a bound of $5-c$ for some $c \geq 0.0157$. To obtain this result, we use a new primal-dual framework to analyze this problem based on a natural semidefinite programming relaxation, together with an online implementation of a correlated randomized rounding procedure of Im and Shadloo (SODA'20). This novel primal-dual framework also yields new, simple and unified proofs of the competitive ratio of the $(3 + 2 \sqrt{2})$-competitive greedy algorithm, the $5$-competitive randomized independent rounding algorithm, and that of a new $4$-competitive optimal fractional algorithm. We also provide lower bounds showing that the previous best randomized algorithm is optimal among independent rounding algorithms, that our new fractional algorithm is optimal, and that a simple greedy algorithm is optimal for the closely related online scheduling problem $R || \sum w_j C_j$.
item.dc:creator: Sander Borst, Danish Kashaev

item.title: Simpler Logarithmic Approximation Algorithms for the Optimal Decision Tree and Adaptive Set Cover
item.description: arXiv:2604.12036v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of constructing a decision tree that identifies an unknown hypothesis from a given ground set, under both average- and worst-case cost. The Optimal Decision Tree (ODT) problem has been extensively studied in the literature, and $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$-approximation guarantees are known for each criterion, including a simultaneous guarantee for both (here $n$ is the number of hypotheses) [ICML]. Although most of the existing algorithm use simple greedy strategies, their analyses rely on intricate arguments. Since ODT is a fundamental problem with wide-ranging applications, we are interested in developing algorithms that are both effective and easy to understand. We present a new greedy algorithm with a simplified analysis that simultaneously achieves approximation factors below $3.65\log_2 n$ for worst-case cost and $7.3\log_2 n$ for average-case cost. Our algorithm for the Optimal Decision Tree behaves greedily with respect to the hereby introduced Separating Subfamily problem which asks for the cheapest subfamily of tests which partitions the hypotheses into pieces of small enough size. We show that the Separating Subfamily can itself be reduced to an instance of the well-known Maximum Coverage problem. At the core of our approach lies exploiting properties of cutting a clique into small pieces, where edges represent pairs of hypotheses to be separated. In the spirit of simplicity, we also provide a new and straightforward application of ODT: an $\mathcal{O}(\log (k\cdot n))$-approximation for the Adaptive Set Cover problem, where $k$ is the number of possible realizations.
item.dc:creator: Micha{\l} Szyfelbein

item.title: CAFS: A Cache-Aware Frequency Sort for Low-Cardinality Integer Data on x86-64
item.description: arXiv:2605.25040v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integer sorts in OLAP engines often run on columns whose cardinality $K$ is much smaller than the array length $N$. After a group-by stage the intermediate key column has $K$ bounded by the number of distinct group keys, and even a column-store scan typically operates on dictionary-encoded categorical fields where $K$ never exceeds a few thousand. A comparison sort on such a column still pays $\Theta(N \log N)$ comparisons, and a radix sort still pays $\Theta(N \cdot B/b)$ byte passes, irrespective of $K$. This paper describes CAFS, an integer sort that does exploit it on x86-64 with AVX2. The algorithm combines a SIMD bucket sized to one cache line, a Chao1 cardinality estimator over 1024 strided samples (kept in a heap-allocated 40 KB open-addressing table), and an adaptive dispatcher backed by a spill safety guard. The hot loop is branchless and uses AVX2 cmpeq together with movemask and tzcnt to locate the matching lane. We benchmarked CAFS on a full-factorial grid of 58 array sizes $N$ from $10^3$ to $3 \cdot 10^7$ with dense $K$ schedules per $N$, producing 592770 timed runs against pdqsort, IPS4o, vqsort, ska_sort, and std::sort. In the $K \ll N$ band the throughput is 1.7 to 3.1x that of pdqsort, 1.7 to 3.5x IPS4o, and 1.2 to 2.3x vqsort. The operational crossover against pdqsort is at $K \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^5$; against ska_sort, $K \approx 8.14 \cdot 10^5$; against vqsort, $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$; and against IPS4o the curves only converge near $K = N$. Of the five baselines, only vqsort actually overtakes CAFS once the crossover is passed, which makes the vqsort threshold at $K \approx 6.7 \cdot 10^5$ the binding constraint on the operational range of CAFS.
item.dc:creator: Vasiliy S. Shlyk

item.title: Connected (Dense) Partition for Tree-Like Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.22070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We focus on two variants of graph partitioning problems, connected partition and dense partition. Formally, given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a partition of its vertices $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we say that $\mathcal P$ is a connected partition of $G$ if each $P_i$ induces a connected graph in $G$. Many classical variants of this problem impose additional restrictions both on the number of parts as well as on the size of each part. Moreover, given a partition $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots, P_k\}$ we define its density by $d(\mathcal P):=\sum_{i=1}^k |E(P_i)|/|V(P_i)|$. The problem Maximum Dense Graph Partition asks to construct a partition of maximum density. We study this problem both with and without fixed number of sets $k$. We prove the following results: 1. A polynomial time algorithm for \textsc{Maximum Dense Graph Partition} of thick forests, a subclass of chordal graphs, generalizing the previously known polynomial time algorithm on block graphs. 2. A generic dynamic programming algorithm to construct (if possible) a connected partition into $k$ sets of prescribed sizes on graphs with bounded treewidth. This yields algorithms for both variants of Dense Graph Partition and an efficient construction for the Gy\H{o}ri-Lov\'{a}sz theorem. 3. The $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness of Maximum Dense Graph Partition restricted to split graphs, showing that thick trees are a boundary for the polynomial computability of this problem.
item.dc:creator: Katrin Casel, Archontia C. Giannopoulou, Aikaterini Niklanovits

item.title: Nonlinear Exchange Dynamics for Independent Sets
item.description: arXiv:2607.29016v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, nonlinear dynamics derived from kinetic theory have gained attention in the context of sampling configurations of spin systems such as the Ising model. We focus on nonlinear dynamics for the hard-core model, a canonical spin system with hard constraints that specifies a distribution over independent sets in a graph, weighted by their sizes. We explore two distinct types of nonlinear dynamics: the mean-field dynamics, which preserves the density (or average size) of independent sets, and the single-site dynamics, which preserves the marginal vector (i.e., the occupancy probabilities of the vertices). These dynamics are natural stochastic processes for sampling from the hard-core model with a specified density or marginal vector, respectively, both of which are canonical instances of maximum entropy distributions that have been studied in various contexts. In contrast to linear Markov chains, there is a significant lack of a fundamental theoretical framework for nonlinear dynamics. We develop foundational theoretical tools for analyzing nonlinear dynamics within the context of the hard-core model. We establish almost linear convergence of both the mean-field and single-site dynamics at sufficiently low density through novel coupling arguments. We also establish exponential decay of relative entropy for the mean-field dynamics all the way up to the critical density. Additionally, we design new algorithms for sampling from the hard-core distribution with either a specified density or a specified marginal vector. These algorithms are based on a related linear Markov chain, called the particle-system dynamics and inspired by the so-called Kac's program, that approximates the associated nonlinear dynamics. As we demonstrate in the paper, they are comparable in time complexity, but simpler to implement, than traditional approaches based on learning parameter values.
item.dc:creator: Mehrad Abbaszadeh Minab, Pietro Caputo, Zongchen Chen, Mario Morellini, Alistair Sinclair

item.title: Truthful Calibration Measures for Sequential Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2608.21348v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Calibration requires probabilistic reports to be conditionally unbiased and reliably interpretable as probabilities. A calibration measure assigns numerical error to miscalibrated reports. Haghtalab et al. (2024) proposed an approximately truthful calibration measure for online prediction, leaving open whether exact truthfulness is compatible with completeness and soundness. We resolve this question negatively for sequential binary prediction: exact truthfulness is incompatible with completeness and soundness, even for independent outcomes. We then show that this impossibility is specific to exact truthfulness. On the positive side, we give two general reductions that transform a base calibration measure satisfying a uniform completeness condition into additively and multiplicatively approximately truthful measures, respectively. Applying the multiplicative reduction, for every $0<\varepsilon<1$ we construct a sound and complete calibration measure that is $1+\exp\left(-\Omega(T^{1-\varepsilon})\right)$-multiplicatively truthful. This improves the approximate truthfulness guarantee of Haghtalab et al. (2024). We also prove a general transfer theorem showing that the uniform completeness of one calibration measure transfers to another when they are quantitatively related. Using this result, we show that every consistent calibration measure (Blasiok et al., 2023) satisfies uniform completeness and can serve as the base calibration measure to achieve $1 + o(1)$ multiplicative truthfulness.
item.dc:creator: Anagha Gokul, Jason Hartline, Lunjia Hu, Jonathan Ullman, Yifan Wu

item.title: Computing Lewis Weights to High Precision by Fixed-Point Iteration
item.description: arXiv:2609.04338v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The $\ell_p$-Lewis weights of a matrix are defined by a fixed-point equation. For $p<4$, Cohen and Peng [CP15] showed that iterating an equivalent rearrangement of this equation computes Lewis weights to high precision; for $p\geq4$, prior high-precision methods instead use optimization-based approaches. We show that the direct Lewis fixed-point iteration, appearing in the thesis of Lee [Lee16], computes Lewis weights to high precision for every $p>2$. For a matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ partitioned into row blocks $\mathbf{A}_{[1]},\ldots,\mathbf{A}_{[k]}$, we compute, for $p>2$, coordinatewise $\varepsilon$-approximate $\ell_p$ block Lewis weights in $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}_{[i]})}}{\varepsilon}\right)$ rounds of exact leverage-score-vector computations. For ordinary Lewis weights, this becomes $O\left(p\log\frac{p\sqrt{m}}{\varepsilon}\right)$, improving the $O\left(p^2\log(m/\varepsilon)\right)$ bound of Gribling, Sidford, and Zhang [GSZ26] for $p\geq4$. Our guarantees also extend to approximate leverage-score computations. Our main observation is that each direct Lewis update contracts the KL divergence to the true weights by a factor of $1-\frac{2}{p}$. We also give an alternate explanation of this contraction through volume sampling and entropic independence. Synthetic experiments closely match our predicted local contraction rates and iteration counts grow approximately linearly with $p$; real-data experiments illustrate the information-concentration tradeoff of finite-$p$ block Lewis designs.
item.dc:creator: Swati Padmanabhan

item.title: The Complexity of Weak Partition Connectivity in Hedgegraphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.14932v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that deciding whether the weak partition connectivity (WPC) of an unweighted hedgegraph is at most a given integer is NP-complete, resolving an open question about its computational complexity. Hardness holds even for connected full-support split systems, where each hedge consists of two nonempty, vertex-disjoint hyperedges covering all vertices. We also obtain hardness on connected edge-colored simple graphs in which each color class is a spanning forest with exactly two nontrivial trees. On both classes, exact computation of fractional WPC is NP-hard, whereas hedge connectivity is computable exactly in polynomial time. A binary matrix formulation yields the reduction and a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm under a linear intersection condition on row supports after normalization and column compression. In particular, both integer and fractional WPC are computable in polynomial time when these supports have size at most two, whereas NP-hardness holds already when their size is bounded by three. For every fixed $b$, we give deterministic and randomized efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes on hedgegraphs in which each hedge has at most $b$ connected components, counting isolated vertices. Both schemes return one partition that simultaneously approximates integer and fractional WPC. Unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, neither objective admits a deterministic FPTAS, even on the two hard instance classes.
item.dc:creator: Yuanhao Wang, Wei Wang

item.title: Approximating Prize-Collecting TSP below 1.556
item.description: arXiv:2609.24944v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The prize-collecting traveling salesperson problem is a variant of the metric traveling salesperson problem in which vertices may be left unvisited by paying their associated penalties. The objective is to minimize the length of the tour plus the total penalty of the unvisited vertices. Blauth, Klein, and N\"agele gave the previously best-known LP-relative $1.599$-approximation. Their algorithm constructs tours by applying a splitting-off preprocessing to an LP solution, decomposing the resulting solution into trees, pruning them, and performing parity correction. We improve the LP-relative approximation ratio to $1.55576$. Our main contribution is a new bound on the cost of parity correction that exploits parity information revealed by further pruning in the analysis. This bound makes the splitting-off preprocessing unnecessary, so the improvement is achieved by a simpler version of their algorithm. The stated factor follows from a numerical parameter search with exact verification, while an elementary analysis already yields an LP-relative $1.56$-approximation.
item.dc:creator: Hong Li

item.title: Practical and Space-Efficient LZ77 and LZ Pre-Compression via String Synchronizing Sets
item.description: arXiv:2609.30193v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Lempel-Ziv (LZ77) factorization decomposes a text into the least possible number $z$ of phrases that each refer to an earlier occurrence. It is this phrase count, rather than the encoded size, that governs the size of LZ-based compressed indexes, and computing a factorization with few phrases is a time and space bottleneck in their construction. In practice, computing LZ77 quickly typically requires the suffix array. In theory, the exact LZ77 factorization, and a 3-approximation of it, can be computed more space-efficiently without the full suffix array [SPIRE 2023]. These algorithms have remained unimplemented, because two of their components resist a direct implementation: a lookup table that degenerates to patterns of length at most two for realistic inputs, and an orthogonal range reporting data structure that is impractical. We replace both, fine-tune every remaining stage, and obtain the first practical implementation, which runs in space close to the text rather than to the suffix array. On one thread, our 3-approximation factorizes 12-19x faster than the classical LPF algorithm while using 14x less memory; on 32 threads, even our exact algorithm is 1.4-2.9x faster than parallel LPF, at 9x less memory. In practice the approximation ratio stays far below 3. As a side result, passing only the perfect phrases of our 3-approximation to a downstream compressor yields a precompressor that is on par with the state of the art [Dinklage, SEA 2026] in compression ratio, and better in memory consumption and parallel throughput.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Ellert, Lukas Nalbach

item.title: Near-Optimal Bounds for Testing Residual-String Equality and Parenthesis Languages
item.description: arXiv:2609.35746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Residual-String Equality, denoted $\texttt{ResStringEq}$, is the property consisting of all pairs of strings over $\{0,1,*\}$ that are equal after deleting all `$*$' symbols from them. This property was first introduced by Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA 2018), who used it to show a lower bound on testing the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, where $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ is the language consisting of balanced sequences of parentheses over $m$ parenthesis types. They showed that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ on inputs of length $n$ requires $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ queries, and presented a reduction from testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ to testing $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ for any $m \geq 2$. Furthermore, they showed that $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ can be tested with $O(n^{2/5+\delta})$ queries for every constant proximity parameter, where $\delta>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant. In this work, we nearly close the gap, by showing that testing $\texttt{ResStringEq}$, and hence $\texttt{Dyck}_m$ (for any $m\geq 2$), requires $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ queries. We also show a stronger lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for testers that make non-adaptive queries. We establish that the $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ bound is nearly tight, by presenting a non-adaptive tester for $\texttt{ResStringEq}$ that uses $O(n^{1/2+\delta})$ queries for an arbitrarily small constant $\delta>0$. Furthermore, we extend this non-adaptive tester to the $\texttt{Dyck}$ languages, with the same query complexity. Finally, we improve the dependence on the proximity parameter $\epsilon$ in the tester of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya, reducing it from $O(1/\epsilon)^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\delta)}$ to $O(1/\epsilon)^{O(\log(1/\delta))}$.
item.dc:creator: Hadar Strauss

item.title: Cascade: GPU-Accelerated Out-of-Core Suffix Array Construction for LLM Corpora
item.description: arXiv:2610.15254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Suffix arrays power deduplication, contamination testing, and training data attribution over the corpora used to train large language models, and must be rebuilt for every new corpus or tokenizer. However, constructing them at scale is slow. infini-gram's indexing pipeline takes about two days to process 1.4 trillion tokens on its authors' 128-core CPU server. GPU-accelerated constructors are an order of magnitude faster, but their working sets must fit in GPU memory. Partitioning the corpus only moves this limit to host memory. Sorting the suffixes of one partition needs the ranks of suffixes in other partitions, which existing designs keep in a corpus-wide rank table that must stay in memory. We present Cascade, a GPU-accelerated out-of-core suffix-array constructor. Its partitions each own a fixed, contiguous range of the final suffix array, so the GPU sorts them independently and never merges them. Cascade then replaces the rank table with streamed rank exchange. Ranks are sent directly to the partitions that need them, and an invariant makes partition-local ranks sufficient for every comparison. With no rank table, intermediate data spills across GPU memory, host memory, and SSD as the corpus grows, and host memory only needs to hold the text. On seven corpora of 8-238 billion tokens, Cascade builds suffix arrays on a single GPU server 3.0-8.2x faster end to end than infini-gram's pipeline, and its construction is 6.3-11.4x faster than libsais's. It indexes the 198-billion-token C4 corpus and the 238-billion-token Pile in 23 and 37 minutes end to end, both of which exceed libsais's host-memory capacity on the same server. A batched query engine over the index reproduces infini-gram's counts at median speedups of 10.8-32.6x, with the index in GPU memory, host memory, or on SSD.
item.dc:creator: Jamshed Khan, Prashant Pandey

item.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
item.description: arXiv:2610.19850v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: First defined by Bouchitt\'e and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimo\v{s}ov\'a, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013). Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitt\'e, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth. Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, i.e. a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Berg\'e, Vincent Limouzy, Nicolas Schivre

item.title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
item.description: arXiv:2610.20140v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.
item.dc:creator: Zizong Wang, Yibo Wang, Wenguo Yang

item.title: Assortment optimization given basket shopping behavior using the Ising model
item.description: arXiv:2502.16260v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Vasilyev, Sebastian Maier, Ralf W. Seifert

item.title: Verified Purely Functional Catenable Real-Time Deques
item.description: arXiv:2505.07681v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present OCaml and Rocq implementations of Kaplan and Tarjan's purely functional, real-time catenable deques. The correctness of our Rocq code is machine-checked.
item.dc:creator: Jules Viennot, Arthur Wendling, Arma\"el Gu\'eneau, Fran\c{c}ois Pottier

item.title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2609.31090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $\Theta(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Cristi, Matteo Russo, Jiechen Zhang

item.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.20244v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.
item.dc:creator: Sayan Bandyapadhyay, William Lochet, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue
